studies.headline: The most politically extreme customers are your most loyal — and the least likely to notice a price hike
studies.the_study: Published in the *Journal of Marketing*, this research introduces political extremism — how far toward either end of the ideological spectrum a consumer sits, regardless of direction — as a distinct dimension of polarization affecting post-purchase behavior. Across a multi-study program, consumers with more extreme political identities showed higher repurchase likelihood and notably weaker sensitivity to price increases by brands they had chosen, even when comparable alternatives were available. The mechanism was a belief in the superiority of their own consumption choices; effects strengthened when the brand faced consumption-domain threats (product failures, competitor launches) but faded when the threat was political (for example, discovering the brand's politics clashed with their own).
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes political polarization as a loyalty and pricing variable rather than only a left-versus-right targeting question, and flags a consumer-welfare problem: the most committed buyers may be quietly overpaying.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brands segmenting by political leaning may be missing the more commercially relevant axis — identity intensity. Worth testing whether high-conviction customer cohorts show measurably lower price elasticity in your own data, while recognizing that exploiting that insensitivity is exactly the practice regulators and critics would seize on.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Strong political conviction appears to spill into shopping: people who hold intense ideological identities defend their brand choices as superior and swallow price increases others would walk away from. A useful prompt to check whether your loyalty to a brand is actually saving you money.
studies.caveats: The abstract does not specify sample sizes, populations or whether studies used real purchases; effects on price sensitivity appear to be measured in experimental settings rather than observed market behavior.
studies.paper_title: EXPRESS: Political Extremism and Post-Purchase Customer–Brand Relationships

studies.headline: "High protein" doesn't make shoppers think a food is healthier — it makes them think it's more processed
studies.the_study: In an online experiment (N=218), participants evaluated five food products shown either with or without a "high-protein" front-of-pack label and rated perceived calories, healthiness, sugar, additives, processing level and purchase intention. The label produced no general health halo: it did not shift perceived healthiness, calories, sugar or purchase intent. Instead, labeled products were judged to contain more additives and to be more industrially processed — a "horn" effect — with calorie and sugar inferences shifting mainly for high-calorie products, and existing attitudes toward protein products moderating responses throughout.
studies.why_it_matters: Protein claims have proliferated across categories on the assumption they signal virtue; this suggests the claim can instead cue "engineered food" for a meaningful share of shoppers.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before stamping "high protein" across a portfolio, test the claim against a no-claim control on processing and additive perceptions, not just on appeal — and segment by how enthusiastic your buyers already are about protein, since prior attitude did more work than the label itself.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Shoppers may be getting more skeptical than food marketers assume: a protein flag on the pack can read as a sign the product has been reformulated in a factory rather than as a badge of health.
studies.caveats: Single online experiment with 218 participants; hypothetical product evaluations and stated purchase intention rather than real purchases; five products only; country and panel source not specified in the abstract.
studies.paper_title: Halo or horn? The role of prior attitudes in shaping consumer responses to high-protein food labels

studies.headline: Serve spicy food on an angular plate: shape-taste matching lifts how diners rate a dish
studies.the_study: Four online experiments with 754 valid Chinese respondents spanning all seven major geographic regions tested whether plateware shape should match a dish's pungency. Pungent foods drew more favorable evaluations and higher ordering intention when shown on angular rather than round plates, while mild foods did better on round plates. Processing fluency — how easily the pairing is mentally processed — mediated the effect.
studies.why_it_matters: Plateware is one of the cheapest levers a restaurant or food brand controls, and this suggests matching plate geometry to a dish's sensory profile can shift appeal at essentially no cost.
studies.story_angle_primary: A low-risk A/B test for restaurant groups, meal-kit photography and delivery-app menu imagery: pair angular plates with spicy items and round plates with mild ones, and check whether ordering rates move. Note these were image-based online studies, so in-venue replication is the real test.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Your senses cross-talk more than you think — the outline of the plate under a curry can nudge how appetizing it looks before you have tasted anything.
studies.caveats: Online experiments using depicted rather than eaten food; ordering intention rather than actual orders; all participants Chinese, and shape-taste associations may not transfer across cuisines and cultures.
studies.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
studies.paper_title: When plateware shape matters: The congruence effects between food pungency and plateware shape on food preference

studies.headline: New Year shoppers want coupons; year-end shoppers want discounts
studies.the_study: Three preregistered experiments tested how "temporal landmarks" — the start versus the end of a calendar period, manipulated via dates, weekdays and time of day — shape preference for two economically similar promotions: a coupon versus a straight discount. Consumers at start landmarks preferred coupon framing; those at end landmarks preferred discount framing, with mindset mediating the effect. Product type reversed the pattern: for hedonic goods the coupon-at-start, discount-at-end rule held, while for utilitarian goods it flipped.
studies.why_it_matters: Retailers routinely treat coupons and percentage-off discounts as interchangeable mechanics; this suggests the calendar moment and product category together determine which one lands better.
studies.story_angle_primary: Test promotion mechanics against the calendar, not just against depth of offer — try coupon-led campaigns at January, Monday and month-start moments for indulgence categories, discount-led at period-end for the same, and the reverse for everyday staples.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Fresh-start moments change what feels like a good deal. The same money off can appeal or fall flat depending on whether you feel you are opening a new chapter or closing one out.
studies.caveats: Experimental studies with hypothetical offers and stated preferences rather than observed redemption; sample sizes and participant sources not specified in the abstract; mix of real and fictional brands.
studies.paper_title: Start fresh or end smart? How temporal landmarks influence price reduction strategies

studies.headline: Beauty filters widen the gap between how you look and how you want to look — and raise interest in cosmetic surgery
studies.the_study: Drawing on self-discrepancy theory, this research tested how augmented reality face filters of the kind found on Snapchat and Instagram affect users' views of their actual versus ideal selves. Filter use enlarged the ideal-actual attractiveness gap, which produced psychological discomfort, which in turn predicted greater propensity toward cosmetic surgery and lower self-acceptance; body image moderated the first link. Analysis used the Hayes PROCESS macro on a hypothesized mediation-moderation model.
studies.why_it_matters: AR filters are a standard engagement and try-on feature for beauty and fashion brands, and this is among the first empirical evidence linking them to measurable self-concept harm and surgical intent.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brands and platforms deploying AR beauty tools should anticipate scrutiny of the wellbeing case, not just the conversion case: the authors suggest warning or educational messaging, and there is an untested commercial question of whether "unfiltered" try-on modes build more trust than beautifying ones.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The filtered version of your face may not be harmless fun — it can quietly reset what you think you should look like, and the discomfort that follows is what pushes some people toward considering surgery.
studies.caveats: Sample size, country and recruitment source are not reported in the abstract; the design appears cross-sectional and survey-based, so causal direction and long-term effects are unestablished — the authors themselves call for longitudinal work.
studies.paper_title: Examining the impact of augmented reality face filters on consumers’ self-concept and well-being

studies.headline: Electric delivery vans may be quietly pushing customers toward cheeseburgers
studies.the_study: Across six experiments, including two field studies, researchers tested how advertising a food delivery order as sustainable — delivered by electric vehicle — changed what people ordered. When delivery was framed as green, consumers felt less guilt about the meal itself and shifted toward more indulgent, less healthy options. The effect was stronger when shoppers had to pay extra for the sustainable delivery, suggesting that paying for the green option buys a bigger moral license.
studies.why_it_matters: A sustainability feature attached to the service layer of a transaction spilled over into the product itself, nudging up unhealthy consumption — an unintended consequence for delivery platforms, restaurants and public health bodies promoting green logistics.
studies.story_angle_primary: Delivery platforms and restaurant brands promoting electric fleets should test whether the green badge is changing basket composition, not just brand perception — and consider whether pairing sustainability messaging with health cues, or decoupling the green fee from checkout, dampens the licensing effect. The field studies make this more than a lab curiosity, but effect sizes at commercial scale remain unproven.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A useful self-check for anyone who orders in: the feeling of having done something virtuous — recycling, walking to the store, paying extra for the eco option — can quietly loosen restraint on the next decision. The van being electric says nothing about what's inside the bag.
studies.caveats: Mix of online experiments and two field studies; the paper does not report sample sizes or countries in the abstract, and food delivery is a single category. Guilt is a self-reported mechanism.
studies.paper_title: “Green wheels and guilty pleasures”: the impact of sustainable delivery on unhealthy food ordering

studies.headline: People on GLP-1 drugs show a gut-level preference for healthy food — and don't know it
studies.the_study: Researchers compared implicit and explicit food evaluations of GLP-1 medication users and non-users, using the Implicit Association Test with two different sets of evaluative terms: one about enjoyment and taste, the other about desirability. Medication users showed significantly stronger implicit preferences for healthy foods when the terms related to enjoyment and taste, an effect driven by semaglutide users rather than tirzepatide users. Explicit ratings of healthiness, tastiness and irresistibility did not differ between groups, implying users are not consciously aware of the shift.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests GLP-1 drugs may not just suppress appetite but change what food feels enjoyable at an automatic level — which would reshape how food brands should talk to a fast-growing segment of customers.
studies.story_angle_primary: Food and beverage brands building GLP-1 strategies typically assume smaller portions and higher protein; this hints the deeper opportunity is taste and pleasure positioning around healthy options, since users may find them genuinely more appealing without saying so on a survey. Worth testing directly with sensory and purchase data rather than stated preference research, and worth watching whether the effect differs by drug.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If you're on one of these medications and find yourself reaching for the salad, it may not be willpower — your automatic taste associations may have moved without you noticing, which is why self-reported cravings are a poor guide to what you'll actually eat.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional comparison of users and non-users, so it cannot establish that the medication caused the shift (people who choose these drugs may differ to begin with); sample size and country not stated in the abstract; implicit association measures are noisy predictors of real-world eating; the semaglutide versus tirzepatide contrast rests on subgroup comparisons.
studies.paper_title: GLP-1 medication use is associated with stronger implicit preferences for healthy foods based on enjoyment and taste

studies.headline: Consumers file "cell-based sausage" by how it was made, not by what it is
studies.the_study: A total of 154 German-speaking omnivores in Switzerland freely sorted 24 written product concepts — animal-based items such as sausage, plus explicitly labeled plant-based and cell-based versions — into groups of their own choosing, with no images or products involved. Multidimensional scaling and cluster analysis showed that people organized the concepts primarily by production method and biological source rather than by food type, and the pattern was similar for men and women.
studies.why_it_matters: Prior research suggests alternatives are adopted more readily when consumers mentally file them in the same category as the conventional product; these results indicate explicit "cell-based" labeling does the opposite, carving out a separate mental category.
studies.story_angle_primary: For companies commercializing cultivated meat and fish, the wording on the pack may determine whether the product competes inside the meat category or sits in a novelty ghetto of its own — a case for testing label formats, adjacency on shelf and visual presentation before regulation locks terminology in place.
studies.story_angle_secondary: How a food is described shapes where it sits in your head before you ever taste it: told something was grown from cells, shoppers stopped thinking "sausage" and started thinking "lab."
studies.caveats: Single country (German-speaking Switzerland), modest sample of 154, omnivores only; participants sorted written concepts with no images, tasting or actual purchases, so it measures mental categorization rather than buying behavior.
studies.paper_title: Categorization of explicitly labeled cell-, plant-, and animal-based food concepts by German-speaking omnivores in Switzerland

studies.headline: Free vegetable-rich school lunches changed nothing — because the kids didn't eat them
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a controlled quasi-experiment across six Dutch primary schools: three schools served vegetable-rich lunches three days a week to children aged 7–13, three acted as controls. Before and after, they measured cognition, wellbeing, food neophobia, food literacy and skin carotenoid levels (a biomarker of vegetable intake, via the Veggie Meter). There were no significant differences between groups on any measure; if anything, food neophobia fell in the control group but not the intervention group. The authors attribute the null result to low meal acceptance, social dynamics at the table, and the cultural unfamiliarity of a warm lunch at school in the Netherlands.
studies.why_it_matters: A well-intentioned, well-funded healthy-food program can produce zero measurable benefit if the product itself isn't accepted — the distribution problem is solved long before the consumption problem is.
studies.story_angle_primary: A textbook case of trial without adoption: supply and availability are not the same as uptake. For anyone launching a health-positive product or reformulation, this argues for testing acceptance and gradual familiarization first — and for measuring actual consumption, not distribution, as the success metric.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Handing children vegetables doesn't make them eat vegetables. Habit, peer pressure and what food 'should' look like at lunchtime appear to matter more than what's on the plate — which is why abrupt dietary switches at home often fail too.
studies.caveats: Quasi-experimental, not randomized; only six schools in one country; short intervention period; null findings may reflect insufficient dose and implementation rather than an ineffective concept; the positive associations reported (carotenoid status with wellbeing, meal liking) are exploratory and correlational.
studies.paper_title: Growing appetites: the impact of vegetable-rich school meals on child nutrition, cognition, and well-being

studies.headline: Ads run during wartime were judged more trustworthy — and lifted brands more than peacetime ads
studies.the_study: Researchers compared television advertising during the first month of a war with a matched routine period, combining advertising expenditure data, consumer attitude measures and a content analysis of the ads themselves. Total ad spending fell sharply, with health and financial services holding relatively steady while food, fashion and leisure dropped significantly. Wartime ads were rated as more reliable and were linked to stronger brand evaluations; routine-period ads were rated as more entertaining but also more irritating. Content analysis showed a wartime shift toward informational and socially oriented messaging.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers rare evidence on what happens to advertising effectiveness when brands pull back during a national crisis — the survivors in the break faced less clutter and were received more credibly.
studies.story_angle_primary: The instinct in a crisis is to go dark. This data suggests the opposite trade-off is worth modeling: as competitors withdraw and tone shifts to informational and community-oriented messaging, the ads that remain may be perceived as more reliable and lift brand evaluations. Treat it as a hypothesis to test against your own crisis-period tracking, not a universal rule.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Viewers don't judge ads by a fixed standard. The same jokey, high-gloss commercial that reads as entertaining in normal times reads as irritating in a national emergency — and a plain informational ad that would normally be forgettable suddenly reads as honest.
studies.caveats: Single country and a single crisis period observed over one month; attitude measures are self-reported evaluations rather than sales; the comparison period is matched but not randomized, so wider contextual changes cannot be ruled out; findings may not generalize to other types of crisis or other media.
studies.paper_title: Television advertising in national crises: shifting consumer attitudes and brand perceptions during the first month of war

studies.headline: When an AI 'doctor' gives health advice, numbers beat stories — up to a point
studies.the_study: Across three experiments in online health communication settings, participants received health information from digital human doctors using either statistical evidence or anecdotal evidence. Statistical evidence increased willingness to adopt the information, and the effect ran through lower perceived deceptiveness — the numbers made the AI presenter feel less like it was trying to manipulate them. The advantage disappeared when the information came from a 'mirrored' digital human (a digital replica of a real person) rather than a purely virtual one.
studies.why_it_matters: Health brands, pharmacies and insurers increasingly deploy AI avatars to deliver advice, and this suggests the evidence style and the avatar's provenance interact: what persuades from a synthetic presenter is not what persuades from a digital twin of a real clinician.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are piloting AI presenters in health or wellness content, treat evidence format as a variable to test alongside avatar design. The signal here is that synthetic-looking presenters may need statistics to buy credibility, while replicas of real humans can carry anecdote — worth validating in live content before rolling it out.
studies.story_angle_secondary: People appear to apply a suspicion discount to AI-delivered health claims, and hard numbers are what lowers it. A vivid patient story from a machine reads as a sales pitch; a percentage reads as a fact.
studies.caveats: Lab-style online experiments with hypothetical health messages rather than real medical decisions or behavior; sample sizes, recruitment source and country are not specified in the abstract; measures stated adoption intentions rather than observed health actions.
studies.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
studies.paper_title: Statistical or anecdotal? How digital human doctors' message evidence influences the effectiveness of online health science popularization

studies.headline: 116 studies later: why alcohol awareness campaigns change minds but not drinking
studies.the_study: Researchers synthesized evidence from 116 studies of alcohol harm-reduction campaigns to work out why such campaigns reliably move awareness and attitudes yet rarely produce lasting behavior change. They propose a "Limits and Levers" framework built on four mechanisms: alignment (message-audience fit), psychological activation (emotion, efficacy, resistance), social amplification (norms and peer diffusion), and structural integration (media and environmental conditions). The central finding is that standalone campaigns underperform, while communication embedded in wider systems of influence, such as pricing, availability and peer norms, does better.
studies.why_it_matters: Public-health and CSR-funded advertising budgets are frequently spent on awareness campaigns evaluated on recall and attitude shifts, metrics this synthesis suggests are poor predictors of actual drinking behavior.
studies.story_angle_primary: For anyone commissioning or buying behavior-change advertising, the practical question shifts from "is the creative good?" to "what else is in place to convert intent into action?" Worth testing campaigns that are deliberately paired with environmental or retail-level changes, and worth reconsidering KPIs that stop at awareness.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It's a useful lens on why the anti-drinking ad you remember vividly never changed what you ordered at the bar: messages compete with price, availability and the drinking norms of the people around you.
studies.caveats: This is an evidence synthesis and conceptual framework rather than new primary data; the underlying studies vary in design, country and campaign type, and the framework itself has not been tested prospectively.
studies.paper_title: The Limits and Levers of Influence: What Works in Alcohol Harm-Reduction Campaigns

studies.headline: Nostalgic packaging nudges people to waste less food, Chinese experiments suggest
studies.the_study: Two online experiments run on the Credamo platform in early 2026 with 456 participants across Chinese provinces (N=196 and N=260) tested whether retro-styled food packaging affects intentions to reduce food waste. Retro designs raised waste-reduction intentions, working through two parallel routes: a sense of "groundedness" and perceptions of the effort behind the food. A follow-up showed that consumers' perceived subjective social status moderated both pathways, so the effect was not uniform across the sample.
studies.why_it_matters: It points to a near-zero-cost design lever, packaging aesthetics, that may influence how carefully consumers treat food after purchase, an area brands usually treat as outside their control.
studies.story_angle_primary: Packaging teams could run in-market tests of nostalgic or heritage-styled designs against current art, measuring not just purchase but post-purchase outcomes like portion finishing or leftover use. The status moderation also suggests the effect may need segment-level testing rather than a blanket rollout.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The look of a package appears to change how much effort you think went into the food inside, and that in turn changes how willing you are to throw it away.
studies.caveats: Online panel participants in a single country; stated intentions rather than measured waste; hypothetical packaging stimuli rather than real purchases; short time horizon.
studies.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
studies.paper_title: How retro packaging design influences consumers' intentions to reduce food waste

studies.headline: The most effective men's health program may be the one that never mentions health
studies.the_study: Researchers conducted semi-structured and pitch-side interviews with 33 men across two sites of the Football Cooperative, an Irish social enterprise using recreational football to reach men who avoid conventional health services, and analyzed them using reflexive thematic analysis and Schein's organizational culture framework. They found that football functions as a taken-for-granted part of masculine identity and requires no health framing at all to draw men in. Health and social benefits followed when the program's design, reliability and inclusive norms aligned with what the men already valued.
studies.why_it_matters: For health communicators and social marketers, it suggests the barrier is often the health frame itself, which carries social risk, rather than a lack of information or motivation.
studies.story_angle_primary: Anyone trying to reach hard-to-engage audiences might test "host the thing they already love" over "advertise the benefit": embed the offer in an existing cultural ritual and let outcomes follow, rather than leading with health messaging that signals vulnerability.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Men who would never book a check-up will show up every week for a kickabout, and the friendships and fitness arrive as a by-product rather than the pitch.
studies.caveats: Qualitative interviews with 33 men at two sites of a single Irish initiative; no health outcomes measured; self-selected participants who were already attending.
studies.paper_title: Health follows football: a reflexive thematic analysis of culture, masculinity, and men’s wellbeing in recreational football

studies.headline: Kids know sugar is bad for them. They just really like it
studies.the_study: Researchers ran six focus groups with 44 fourth-grade primary school children across two schools, asking about their motivations for eating sugar, where sugary foods are most available, and the roles of family and school. The children could readily identify sugar sources and name health consequences, but described consumption as driven by sensory pleasure and emotional attachment to sweets. Findings were mapped onto the COM-B behavior framework, showing capability (knowledge), opportunity (family and school contexts) and motivation (sensory appeal) each act as both barrier and facilitator.
studies.why_it_matters: It undercuts the assumption behind much child-focused nutrition communication, that more information will change behavior, and points instead at availability and hedonic appeal as the levers that matter.
studies.story_angle_primary: For food and beverage brands and public-health campaigners alike, the takeaway is that education-only messaging to children is likely to fail; the actionable variables are where sugary products appear in a child's day and whether reduced-sugar alternatives can compete on taste and fun.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Children as young as nine can explain why sugar is bad for them and eat it anyway, which is a fairly good description of most adults' relationship with food too.
studies.caveats: Small qualitative study, 44 children in two schools, single country; focus groups capture stated views, not observed eating; group dynamics may shape what children say.
studies.paper_title: Life (without sweets) would be black and white: Exploring primary school children's views on eating practices and sugar consumption

studies.headline: Can a VR headset make people want to volunteer abroad?
studies.the_study: A four-study program combining netnography, an experiment, focus groups and structural modeling examined whether virtual reality promotional content increases willingness to engage in voluntourism. VR raised willingness indirectly, through perceived authenticity and curiosity, but the authenticity route weakened among people high in cultural adventurousness and "aspiring indulger" orientation. Self-congruence predicted willingness positively, while a sense of moral obligation predicted it negatively, and willingness itself was positively related to psychological wellbeing.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests immersive promotional content works on prosocial offers by sparking curiosity and a sense of realness, and that guilt-based moral appeals may actively backfire.
studies.story_angle_primary: Travel, charity and cause marketers experimenting with immersive content could test curiosity-led and identity-led framings against obligation-led ones, and watch for the finding that the most worldly, adventure-seeking segments respond least to authenticity cues.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The finding that feeling obligated makes people less willing to sign up is a reminder of how easily guilt-based appeals from charities can push people away rather than draw them in.
studies.caveats: Willingness and stated intentions rather than actual volunteering or bookings; mixed-method design with limited detail on sample sizes and sourcing; wellbeing link is correlational.
studies.paper_title: Exploring the impact of virtual reality on voluntourism engagement and well-being

studies.headline: When a disease is brand new, telling people how likely they are to catch it beats describing the symptoms
studies.the_study: Across three experiments, researchers tested how two kinds of information — the odds of contracting a disease and the severity of its symptoms — drive information seeking and preventive intentions such as vaccination. For "truly novel" diseases like COVID-19 in its early days, where infection risk is knowable but consequences are not, only probability information moved behavior; descriptions of symptoms and consequences did not. Emphasizing probability in the message raised preventive intentions for novel diseases, but had no such effect for familiar, well-understood illnesses.
studies.why_it_matters: Public health campaigns and health brands routinely lead with vivid depictions of what a disease does to you; this evidence suggests that for an unfamiliar threat, the more persuasive lever is simply how likely you are to get it.
studies.story_angle_primary: Health communicators and pharma marketers could test probability-led messaging against consequence-led messaging in early-stage outbreak or new-vaccine campaigns — and note that the same framing appears to add nothing for established diseases, where the playbook may need to flip. These are controlled experiments, so the effect size in a real campaign is an open question.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It's a window into how we process unfamiliar risk: when we can't picture the outcome, we anchor on the odds instead — which helps explain why early pandemic messaging about case rates landed harder than descriptions of symptoms.
studies.caveats: Experimental studies with hypothetical scenarios and stated behavioral intentions rather than observed vaccination or prevention behavior; sample composition and country not specified in the abstract.
studies.paper_title: Communication of truly novel diseases (TNDS) and preventative behavior

studies.headline: AI companions make users feel better and more exposed at the same time
studies.the_study: Researchers combined a netnography of 1,131 online posts with a survey of 610 users of AI companion apps to map how emotional dependence on these products affects wellbeing. The warmth and constant availability of an AI companion produced a "positive" dependence that reduced felt vulnerability and improved wellbeing. But the AI's emotional capabilities — combined with the fact that a third-party company controls the relationship — increased users' sense of a power imbalance, raising vulnerability and lowering wellbeing.
studies.why_it_matters: Companion AI is becoming a consumer category, and this suggests the very features that make it engaging (emotional responsiveness, always-on availability) are also what make users feel exposed to the company behind the app.
studies.story_angle_primary: For anyone building or partnering with emotionally responsive AI products, the finding points to a design and governance question worth testing: can protective features — transparency about company control, coping and self-worth supports, user input into the product — retain the warmth benefit while defusing the power-imbalance harm? Expect regulators and journalists to press on who owns the relationship.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For users, the discomfort many feel about an AI friend isn't irrational: the study puts a name to it — a company, not the companion, holds the controls, and the more emotionally capable the AI, the sharper that asymmetry feels.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey plus social-media posts, so causal direction cannot be established; self-selected users of companion apps; platform and country coverage not specified in the abstract.
studies.paper_title: Feeling Vulnerable With My AI Companion: Examining Well‐Being in Human‐AI Relationships

studies.headline: In rural areas, opaque bank algorithms push people out of banking — unless the community pushes back
studies.the_study: A two-part study examined how algorithmic opacity in financial services affects remote communities in North America and Europe: 32 in-depth interviews across eight peripheral regions (Nunavut, Yukon, Appalachia, Northern Maine, the Scottish Highlands and Islands, Lapland, Galicia, the Eastern Carpathians), followed by a survey of 575 residents modeled with structural equation modeling. Opaque algorithms and weak AI governance were linked to perceptions of "digital redlining" and financial anxiety, eroding trust and driving withdrawal from banking. Community empowerment buffered the effect: in digitally literate, well-connected communities, people read algorithmic failures as a systemic problem rather than a personal one and stayed engaged.
studies.why_it_matters: Banks automating credit and service decisions may be quietly losing whole geographies of customers, and the mitigating factor is not just better algorithms but whether local communities can interpret rejections collectively.
studies.story_angle_primary: Financial services marketers should look at withdrawal and disengagement rates by geography, not just by segment, and test whether local explanation efforts — plain-language decision reasons, community partnerships, digital literacy programs — measurably retain customers where automated decisioning is dense.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A quietly reassuring finding for consumers: people who talk to their neighbors about being turned down by an algorithm are less likely to blame themselves — and less likely to give up on banking altogether.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey for the quantitative portion, so causation cannot be established; self-reported perceptions and intentions rather than observed account closures; eight specific rural regions that may not generalize to urban or Global South contexts.
studies.paper_title: Algorithmic opaqueness to financial disengagement: buffering role of community well-being in AI anxiety and perceived redlining across rural regions in the Global North

studies.headline: Financial anxiety hurts men and women's wellbeing in exactly the same way
studies.the_study: Using the 2021 US National Financial Capability Study, researchers modeled financial anxiety as the link between financial capability and financial wellbeing among American adults. Higher capability predicted lower anxiety and higher wellbeing, with anxiety carrying a significant share of the effect. A multi-group analysis found the mechanism was gender-invariant: despite women typically reporting higher anxiety levels, the pathway from capability to wellbeing via anxiety worked identically for men and women.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges a common assumption in financial services marketing and financial education that women need structurally different programs — the difference appears to be in levels of anxiety, not in how anxiety operates.
studies.story_angle_primary: Banks and fintechs segmenting financial wellness content by gender may be solving the wrong problem: the evidence suggests targeting emotional barriers directly, for everyone, rather than building parallel gendered products. Worth testing whether anxiety-reducing messaging outperforms knowledge-only content in live campaigns.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Financial know-how doesn't just help you make better decisions — it helps mostly by making you less anxious, and that route to feeling better about money works the same regardless of gender.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional secondary survey data, so causation cannot be established; single country (United States); self-reported measures; a single survey wave (2021), during pandemic-era financial conditions.
studies.paper_title: Financial anxiety as a pathway linking financial capability and financial well-being: a test of gender differences

fact_check.headline: The most politically extreme customers are your most loyal — and the least likely to notice a price hike
fact_check.notes: Faithful to the abstract's mechanism, moderators and welfare framing; headline paraphrase of price insensitivity as "not noticing" is loose.

issues.label: Headline paraphrase of price insensitivity
issues.as_written: the least likely to notice a price hike
issues.abstract_says: they are also less sensitive to price increases by their chosen brands, even when viable alternatives exist
issues.problem: Lower price sensitivity is a response measure, not evidence that extreme consumers fail to perceive or notice price increases; the abstract makes no claim about awareness.
issues.suggested_fix: Reword to "the least likely to walk away from a price hike" or "the least price-sensitive".

issues.label: Number of studies unspecified
issues.as_written: Across a multi-study program, consumers with more extreme political identities showed higher repurchase likelihood
issues.abstract_says: The abstract does not state how many studies were run or what methods were used.
issues.problem: "Multi-study program" implies a known design the abstract does not describe; the digest's own caveat acknowledges this, but the body states it as fact.
issues.suggested_fix: Say "the research reports" and note that the abstract gives no design details.

fact_check.headline: "High protein" doesn't make shoppers think a food is healthier — it makes them think it's more processed
fact_check.notes: N, design, products and horn effect all match; one story angle overstates the relative weight of prior attitudes, and the null moderation by drive for muscularity is dropped.

issues.label: Relative importance of prior attitude overstated
issues.as_written: since prior attitude did more work than the label itself
issues.abstract_says: Attitudes toward protein products moderated the label's effect across nutritional judgments, whereas drive for muscularity did not moderate labeling effects.
issues.problem: The abstract reports moderation, not a comparison of effect magnitudes between attitude and label; "did more work" implies an ordering the abstract does not support.
issues.suggested_fix: Change to "since prior attitude shaped how people read the label".

issues.label: Dropped null moderator
issues.as_written: existing attitudes toward protein products moderating responses throughout
issues.abstract_says: Attitudes toward protein products moderated the label's effect across nutritional judgments, whereas drive for muscularity did not moderate labeling effects.
issues.problem: The abstract's contrast with drive for muscularity (measured, non-significant) is omitted, which is informative for segmentation advice.
issues.suggested_fix: Add that drive for muscularity was measured but did not moderate the label's effect.

fact_check.headline: Serve spicy food on an angular plate: shape-taste matching lifts how diners rate a dish
fact_check.notes: Four online experiments, 754 valid responses, Chinese participants across all seven regions, fluency mediation and the mild-food reversal are all reported correctly; caveats appropriately flag images and intention measures.

fact_check.headline: New Year shoppers want coupons; year-end shoppers want discounts
fact_check.notes: Three preregistered experiments, the manipulations, mindset mediation and the hedonic/utilitarian reversal all match; the headline simplifies but the body carries the boundary condition.

fact_check.headline: Beauty filters widen the gap between how you look and how you want to look — and raise interest in cosmetic surgery
fact_check.notes: Mediation-moderation chain, PROCESS analysis, originality claim and the authors' call for longitudinal work all match the abstract; caveats correctly note undisclosed sample details.

fact_check.headline: Electric delivery vans may be quietly pushing customers toward cheeseburgers
fact_check.notes: Six experiments including two field studies, the guilt mechanism and the delivery-cost moderator are all reported accurately, with appropriately hedged framing.

fact_check.headline: People on GLP-1 drugs show a gut-level preference for healthy food — and don't know it
fact_check.notes: IAT conditions, the enjoyment/taste versus desirability contrast, the semaglutide-versus-tirzepatide pattern and the null explicit ratings all match; caveats correctly flag the cross-sectional design.

fact_check.headline: Consumers file "cell-based sausage" by how it was made, not by what it is
fact_check.notes: Sample, task and analysis match the abstract; the consumer-facing angle reads more into the sorting result than the abstract reports.

issues.label: Consumer angle overreads the sorting data
issues.as_written: told something was grown from cells, shoppers stopped thinking "sausage" and started thinking "lab."
issues.abstract_says: the participants' categorization of the presented written product concepts was primarily influenced by the production method labels and biological source descriptors along three dimensions
issues.problem: The abstract reports categorization dimensions, not that participants formed a "lab" category, and the participants were 154 German-speaking Swiss omnivores rather than shoppers in general.
issues.suggested_fix: Reword to "these participants grouped the concepts by how they were produced rather than by food type".

issues.label: Separate-category inference stated as result
issues.as_written: these results indicate explicit "cell-based" labeling does the opposite, carving out a separate mental category
issues.abstract_says: Prior research has suggested that plant-based alternatives may be more likely to be adopted when they are perceived as belonging to the same category as their animal-based counterparts... results revealed that the participants' categorization... was primarily influenced by the production method labels and biological source descriptors
issues.problem: The abstract stops at describing categorization dimensions and offers the acceptance link only as background; it does not conclude that cell-based labels create a separate category that harms adoption.
issues.suggested_fix: Frame as an implication the authors raise for future research rather than a demonstrated result.

fact_check.headline: Free vegetable-rich school lunches changed nothing — because the kids didn't eat them
fact_check.notes: Design, schools, age range, measures and null results all match; headline states the authors' "most plausible explanation" as established fact, and two descriptors (free, well-funded) are not in the abstract.

issues.label: Headline states explanation as established
issues.as_written: Free vegetable-rich school lunches changed nothing — because the kids didn't eat them
issues.abstract_says: Insufficient meal consumption, driven by low meal acceptance, social dynamics, and cultural unfamiliarity with warm lunches at school, is the most plausible explanation for the absence of effects.
issues.problem: The abstract offers low consumption as the most plausible interpretation, not a measured cause; the body correctly attributes it to the authors, but the headline asserts it.
issues.suggested_fix: Add hedging, e.g. "— most likely because the kids didn't eat them".

issues.label: Unsupported descriptors
issues.as_written: A well-intentioned, well-funded healthy-food program
issues.abstract_says: The abstract describes a school-based lunch programme offering vegetable-rich meals on 3 school days per week but says nothing about cost to families or funding.
issues.problem: "Free" (headline) and "well-funded" are not verifiable from the abstract.
issues.suggested_fix: Drop "free" and "well-funded" or mark as unverifiable from the abstract.

fact_check.headline: Ads run during wartime were judged more trustworthy — and lifted brands more than peacetime ads
fact_check.notes: Spend, sector, attitude and content-analysis findings all match; the headline converts an association into a causal brand lift, and the clutter explanation is the digest's own inference.

issues.label: Causal language in headline
issues.as_written: and lifted brands more than peacetime ads
issues.abstract_says: wartime advertising was perceived as more reliable and was associated with stronger brand evaluations
issues.problem: This is an observational comparison of two periods; "lifted brands" asserts a causal effect on brand outcomes that the abstract describes only as an association with brand evaluations (not sales).
issues.suggested_fix: Reword to "— and were associated with stronger brand evaluations than peacetime ads".

issues.label: Clutter explanation not in abstract
issues.as_written: the survivors in the break faced less clutter and were received more credibly
issues.abstract_says: Advertising spending sharply declines during wartime... wartime advertising was perceived as more reliable
issues.problem: Reduced clutter as the reason for higher perceived reliability is the digest's interpretation; the abstract attributes the pattern to a shift toward informational and socially oriented communication.
issues.suggested_fix: Attribute the mechanism to the content shift the abstract reports, and present the clutter idea explicitly as a hypothesis.

fact_check.headline: When an AI 'doctor' gives health advice, numbers beat stories — up to a point
fact_check.notes: Design and mechanism reported correctly, but the moderation result is described as the whole effect disappearing when the abstract only reports the mediating effect becoming non-significant.

issues.label: Moderator overstated
issues.as_written: The advantage disappeared when the information came from a 'mirrored' digital human (a digital replica of a real person) rather than a purely virtual one.
issues.abstract_says: However, when health information is delivered by mirrored rather than virtual digital humans, this mediating effect becomes non-significant.
issues.problem: The abstract reports that the mediation through perceived deceptiveness became non-significant for mirrored digital humans, not that the persuasive advantage of statistical evidence itself vanished. The digest's phrasing, and the angle claim that "replicas of real humans can carry anecdote," go beyond what is reported.
issues.suggested_fix: Say the mediating route through perceived deceptiveness was no longer significant for mirrored digital humans, and soften the angle to note the mechanism did not hold rather than asserting anecdote works for digital twins.

issues.label: Definition of 'mirrored' digital human
issues.as_written: a 'mirrored' digital human (a digital replica of a real person)
issues.abstract_says: when health information is delivered by mirrored rather than virtual digital humans
issues.problem: The abstract does not define what a mirrored digital human is; the gloss is an assumption.
issues.suggested_fix: Attribute the definition or note it is the authors' terminology, unverifiable from the abstract.

fact_check.headline: 116 studies later: why alcohol awareness campaigns change minds but not drinking
fact_check.notes: Study count, framework and four mechanisms match the abstract; the pricing/availability examples are a reasonable reading of "environmental conditions".

fact_check.headline: Nostalgic packaging nudges people to waste less food, Chinese experiments suggest
fact_check.notes: Samples, platform, dates and mediation/moderation structure all match; headline treats intentions as behavior, though the caveats correct this.

issues.label: Headline implies behavior change
issues.as_written: Nostalgic packaging nudges people to waste less food, Chinese experiments suggest
issues.abstract_says: examines how retro packaging design influences food waste reduction intentions
issues.problem: Only stated waste-reduction intentions were measured, not actual waste; the headline reads as behavioral change.
issues.suggested_fix: Reword to "nudges people to say they'll waste less food" or "lifts waste-reduction intentions".

fact_check.headline: The most effective men's health program may be the one that never mentions health
fact_check.notes: Method, sample (33 interviewees, two sites), analytic approach and themes are reported accurately; headline implies a comparative effectiveness claim the qualitative design cannot make.

issues.label: Comparative effectiveness implied
issues.as_written: The most effective men's health program may be the one that never mentions health
issues.abstract_says: The findings suggest that effective gender-responsive health promotion for men may be dependent on creating cultural conditions which reduce social risk and are familiar to men.
issues.problem: The study is an interpretive qualitative analysis of one initiative; it does not compare programs or measure effectiveness, so "most effective" (even hedged) overstates the design.
issues.suggested_fix: Reframe as "A men's health programme that never mentions health" or "Why football reaches men that health messaging can't".

fact_check.headline: Kids know sugar is bad for them. They just really like it
fact_check.notes: Six focus groups, 44 fourth-graders, two schools and the COM-B mapping all match; a couple of inferences run slightly ahead of an exploratory qualitative study.

issues.label: Prescriptive inference from qualitative data
issues.as_written: the takeaway is that education-only messaging to children is likely to fail; the actionable variables are where sugary products appear in a child's day
issues.abstract_says: These findings indicate that intake can be facilitated (or hindered) by capability (e.g., knowledge of sugar sources), opportunity (e.g., family influences, related learning at school), and motivation (e.g., sensory appeal, affective attachment to sweets).
issues.problem: The abstract frames knowledge/capability as both barrier and facilitator and makes no claim about the failure of education-based messaging; the digest converts exploratory focus-group insight into a directive about what will not work.
issues.suggested_fix: Soften to "suggests information alone may not be enough" and note the study informs, rather than tests, intervention design.

issues.label: Children's age
issues.as_written: Children as young as nine can explain why sugar is bad for them
issues.abstract_says: Six focus groups were conducted across two schools, involving 44 fourth-grade students.
issues.problem: The abstract gives grade level, not ages; the specific age is an inference. Unverifiable from abstract only.
issues.suggested_fix: Say "fourth-grade children" rather than specifying age.

fact_check.headline: Can a VR headset make people want to volunteer abroad?
fact_check.notes: Four-study design and all reported pathways match; the moral-obligation result is upgraded from a negative association into guilt-based appeals "backfiring".

issues.label: Association read as causal backfire
issues.as_written: guilt-based moral appeals may actively backfire
issues.abstract_says: Studies 3 and 4 reveal that self-congruence positively predicts willingness to engage, whereas moral obligation is negatively associated with it.
issues.problem: The abstract reports a negative association between a measured sense of moral obligation and willingness, not an experimental test of guilt-based appeals; saying such appeals "backfire" implies a manipulated causal effect on messaging. The consumer angle repeats this ("feeling obligated makes people less willing to sign up").
issues.suggested_fix: State that felt moral obligation was negatively associated with willingness, and that whether obligation-framed appeals reduce sign-ups remains untested.

fact_check.headline: When a disease is brand new, telling people how likely they are to catch it beats describing the symptoms
fact_check.notes: Three experiments, the probability-vs-consequence result and the known-disease boundary condition are all reported correctly, with intentions properly caveated.

fact_check.headline: AI companions make users feel better and more exposed at the same time
fact_check.notes: Netnography (1,131 posts) and survey (610) figures and both dependence pathways match the abstract; cross-sectional limitation is flagged.

fact_check.headline: In rural areas, opaque bank algorithms push people out of banking — unless the community pushes back
fact_check.notes: Interview and survey samples, the eight regions and the community-empowerment moderator are accurate; the headline is more causal than the cross-sectional design and the abstract's hedged wording support.

issues.label: Causal headline for survey data
issues.as_written: In rural areas, opaque bank algorithms push people out of banking — unless the community pushes back
issues.abstract_says: Results show that opaque algorithms and poor governance potentially amplify PRDL and FNAX, eroding institutional trust and promoting withdrawal behaviour.
issues.problem: The quantitative component is a cross-sectional survey and the abstract hedges with "potentially amplify"; the headline asserts a causal push out of banking.
issues.suggested_fix: Hedge the headline, e.g. "are linked to people withdrawing from banking", consistent with the digest's own caveat.

fact_check.headline: Financial anxiety hurts men and women's wellbeing in exactly the same way
fact_check.notes: Data source, mediation result and gender-invariance finding are accurate; the consumer angle overstates how much of the capability–wellbeing link runs through anxiety.

issues.label: Mediation share overstated
issues.as_written: it helps mostly by making you less anxious
issues.abstract_says: financial capability was negatively associated with financial anxiety and positively associated with financial well-being, both directly and indirectly... its mediating role in the capability–well-being link was significant.
issues.problem: The abstract reports significant direct and indirect effects but does not say the indirect (anxiety) route accounts for most of the relationship; "mostly" asserts a magnitude not in the abstract. The body's "anxiety carrying a significant share of the effect" is similarly quantified.
issues.suggested_fix: Say financial capability is linked to wellbeing both directly and partly through lower anxiety, without ranking the routes.

issues.label: Source of level difference
issues.as_written: the difference appears to be in levels of anxiety, not in how anxiety operates
issues.abstract_says: Historically, empirical evidence has suggested that women report higher levels of financial anxiety than men
issues.problem: The higher anxiety levels among women come from prior literature cited as background, not necessarily from this study's own comparison.
issues.suggested_fix: Attribute the level difference to prior research and confine this study's contribution to the gender-invariant mechanism.

sections.trends: _No prior digest on this topic to compare against yet — this is the first run._
sections.feature_pitch:
**The pattern:** A cluster of studies in this batch lands on the same uncomfortable conclusion: telling people what is healthy does almost nothing, because the obstacle is pleasure, availability and social context, not ignorance. "Free vegetable-rich school lunches changed nothing — because the kids didn't eat them" (W7202165920) and "Kids know sugar is bad for them. They just really like it" (W7213326632) show knowledge and supply both failing on their own; "116 studies later: why alcohol awareness campaigns change minds but not drinking" (W7206215832) generalizes it across an entire communications category; and "The most effective men's health program may be the one that never mentions health" (W7213513131) shows what works instead — embedding the behavior in something people already want to do. Two further studies suggest health framing can actively misfire: a "high protein" flag makes shoppers think "processed," not "healthy" (W7208834717), and a green delivery badge loosens restraint on what people order (W7172408085).

**Why pitch this now:** Governments across the UK and Europe are expanding free school meals and tightening junk-food advertising rules on the assumption that supply and messaging shift diets, while public-health and CSR communications budgets are being defended on recall and awareness metrics this evidence says are poor predictors of behavior.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the collapse of the information-deficit model in health marketing — why the best-funded awareness work keeps failing its own evaluation, and what the alternative (design for pleasure, availability and existing rituals) looks like in practice — aimed at marketers, agency strategists and public-health commissioners, with enough human material to carry a general-interest read.

**Potential headlines:**
- Awareness campaigns move attitudes, not behavior — and the research now says why
- The healthiest lunch in the room is the one nobody eats
- Your health messaging budget is buying recall you can't cash

**Potential outlets:**
- **Marketing Week** — its effectiveness coverage would take on the argument that awareness and attitude KPIs are the wrong measure for behavior-change advertising.
- **The Grocer** — directly relevant to reformulation, school-meal policy and the finding that a "high protein" claim can read as "industrially processed" to shoppers.
- **MIT Sloan Management Review** — fits its appetite for evidence-led pieces on program design and why well-funded interventions fail at the adoption stage.
- **The Guardian (food/consumer desk)** — runs school-food and public-health-policy stories with a strong consumer-behavior angle and would use the null school-lunch result as a news hook.
sections.pitch_ideas:
- **The most politically extreme customers are your most loyal — and the least likely to notice a price hike (Work ID W7213535017):** Reframe polarization from a targeting question to a pricing one, with the ethics kicker that brands' most committed buyers may be quietly overpaying, for a CMO-audience column or a consumer-affairs piece in a personal-finance section.
- **"High protein" doesn't make shoppers think a food is healthier (Work ID W7208834717):** The protein boom may have hit its credibility ceiling — the claim now cues additives and factory reformulation rather than virtue, for a food and drink trade explainer or CPG packaging brief.
- **Serve spicy food on an angular plate (Work ID W7212607085):** A near-zero-cost lever for restaurant groups, delivery-app menu photography and meal-kit shoots, with the caveat that it has only been tested on images, for a hospitality or restaurant trade news brief.
- **New Year shoppers want coupons; year-end shoppers want discounts (Work ID W7213550700):** Promotion mechanics should be set by the calendar moment and product type, not just offer depth — a practical January-planning piece, for a retail trade explainer or promotions column.
- **Beauty filters widen the gap between how you look and how you want to look (Work ID W7171940513):** Brands deploying AR try-on now face a wellbeing case as well as a conversion case, and "unfiltered mode" is an untested trust play, for a beauty trade feature or a general-interest health and technology section.
- **Electric delivery vans may be quietly pushing customers toward cheeseburgers (Work ID W7172408085):** Moral licensing at the checkout — paying extra for green delivery buys permission to order worse, backed by field studies, for a sustainability-marketing feature or a consumer-psychology explainer in a general-interest outlet.
- **People on GLP-1 drugs show a gut-level preference for healthy food — and don't know it (Work ID W7213351764):** The food industry's GLP-1 playbook assumes portion size and protein; this suggests the real opening is taste and pleasure positioning on healthy items, with a drug-by-drug difference worth watching, for a food and beverage trade feature or a business-of-health column.
- **Consumers file "cell-based sausage" by how it was made, not by what it is (Work ID W7211919306):** Labeling terminology may decide whether cultivated meat competes inside the meat aisle or in a category of its own — urgent while regulators are still fixing the words, for an agri-food or food-policy trade explainer.
- **Free vegetable-rich school lunches changed nothing (Work ID W7202165920):** A null result with policy teeth as free-school-meal schemes expand: distribution solved, consumption not, for an education or public-health news feature, and a "trial without adoption" lesson for a marketing-strategy column.
- **Ads run during wartime were judged more trustworthy (Work ID W7212377582):** Rare crisis-period evidence that going dark may cost more than staying on air, and that tone — informational, community-oriented — does the work, for an advertising trade analysis piece.
- **When an AI 'doctor' gives health advice, numbers beat stories (Work ID W7212302631):** Synthetic presenters need statistics to buy credibility while digital twins of real clinicians can carry anecdote, a live design question for health and pharma content teams, for a digital-health or health-marketing trade brief.
- **116 studies later: why alcohol awareness campaigns change minds but not drinking (Work ID W7206215832):** A direct challenge to the KPIs used to justify harm-reduction and CSR advertising spend, for an advertising-effectiveness column or a public-health communications outlet.
- **Nostalgic packaging nudges people to waste less food (Work ID W7204661572):** Design as a post-purchase lever — retro art changes how much effort consumers think went into the food and how readily they bin it, for a packaging or sustainability trade brief.
- **The most effective men's health program may be the one that never mentions health (Work ID W7213513131):** The health frame itself is the barrier for hard-to-reach men; embed the offer in an existing ritual instead, for a social-marketing or health-promotion feature, with crossover potential in a sports or men's-interest general outlet.
- **Kids know sugar is bad for them. They just really like it (Work ID W7213326632):** Education-only messaging to children is a dead end; availability and taste competitiveness are the levers, for a parenting or family-health section, or a public-health policy brief.
- **Can a VR headset make people want to volunteer abroad? (Work ID W7171788770):** Curiosity and authenticity recruit volunteers while moral obligation repels them — a warning about guilt-led fundraising creative, for a charity-sector or travel-marketing trade piece.
- **When a disease is brand new, telling people how likely they are to catch it beats describing the symptoms (Work ID W7204799462):** Probability-led framing works for novel threats and adds nothing for familiar ones, a practical split for outbreak and new-vaccine campaigns, for a health-communications trade explainer.
- **AI companions make users feel better and more exposed at the same time (Work ID W7170143709):** The same emotional responsiveness that helps users is what makes the corporate ownership of the relationship feel sinister — a governance story ahead of regulatory attention, for a technology and consumer-wellbeing feature in a general-interest outlet.
- **In rural areas, opaque bank algorithms push people out of banking (Work ID W7170190396):** "Digital redlining" by geography, with community digital literacy as the buffer that keeps people from blaming themselves, for a banking or fintech trade feature, or a rural-affairs section of a general outlet.
- **Financial anxiety hurts men and women's wellbeing in exactly the same way (Work ID W7203676845):** Gendered financial-wellness products may be solving the wrong problem — target the anxiety, not the demographic, for a personal-finance column or a retail-banking marketing brief.
